newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH WHEAT QUALITY FEARS RECEDE.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH WHEAT QUALITY FEARS RECEDE.

text.p: French grain traders are gradually revising down their estimates of the damage caused to wheat by last week's rain.
Hagberg values that help to determine milling quality have not suffered as badly as some had feared despite last week's downpours lasting several days.
Test weight, a combined measure of quantity and quality, is however down significantly this year.
Little firm information was so far available on crop quality, with some tests being kept secret in commercial laboratories.
But traders in the north said most milling varieties would yield a significant proportion of wheat at 220 Hagberg.
That level -- below which wheat can more easily end up in feed -- is generally holding in the northern regions of Picardie and Normandy.
In eastern areas making up five percent of the crop, operators said only a quarter of the wheat harvested in Alsace was on course for milling while in Lorraine the figure was 75 percent.
Milling wheat can vary between 180 and 250 Hagberg, but 220 Hagberg is a benchmark since it is one of the criteria for EU-controlled intervention.
Test weight results were coming in anwhere between 65 and 76 kilos per hectolitre, whereas the usual acceptable standard is 72 kilos.
"We still have a problem with specific weight (test weight) but Hagberg is okay," one trader said.
Premium quality wheat of guaranteed quality had soared up to 100 francs per tonne higher than standard Rouen wheat last week, but traders said the spread was cooling off.

Soft wheat prices were around 870 francs a tonne excluding carrying charges for standard material at Rouen, but there was little interest n Wednesday in bidding separately for guaranteed quality, traders said.
